en: The marten cap upon your head—
Who might not wear it jauntily?
While fortune rests upon one's head,
Who would not go about in splendor?
Youngest of six lions,
Allah's beloved servant,
My Magnanimous Manas, if only you had not died!
If only the sobbing orphan Semetey
Had not come wandering here!
Setting out on the road to Bukhara,
You travelled far in anguish,
Rubbing your calves raw,
Hurting your heels;
The wide world grew narrow.
My mother, who would not ride a mere pacer,
Was reduced to longing for a sore-backed donkey.
Semetey, whom the tiger left behind,
Was abased, wandering through the wilds.
Fleeing the delights of Talas,
You reached the Syr Darya and camped.
Now that I have grown old,
You have killed me before my appointed death,
Drained me away in grief.
Slipping, I have lost my throne,
Parted from my fortune;
You have blunted your steel.
Those I sat relying upon—
My mother and my Kanykei—I have lost!”
So Khan Bakai spoke,
Sobbing bitterly.
His beard was left sparse,
His mustache had been torn out.
His bare head, round as a travel kettle,
Had been struck with a battle-axe.
Precious tears mixed with blood
From grief-stricken Bakai
Poured down over his collarbones.
Wailing in distress,
At the sight of the fugitives
He cried, “My khan Manas, my leopard,
Take me with you!”
“Mother, has a deep pit been dug?
Semetey, whom the Magnanimous left,
Mother, you have taken upon your back.
Has an enemy come from Mecca?
If an enemy has come from Mecca,
If an oppressive demand has been made,
My valiant mother, tell the truth.
Grant me a gray steed to ride;
If an enemy has come from Mecca,
Let me strike toward Mecca.
If an oppressive demand has been made,
My valiant mother, tell the truth.
If an enemy has come from Beijing,
Let me strike straight toward Beijing.
Let me avenge my unforgotten grievance.
Tell the truth; spare me grief.
If another vengeful enemy has come,
Let me offer him in sacrifice.
If my appointed death has come, let me die.
If an enemy would come out to fight,
Tell the truth, mother;
Let me fight and take revenge!”
While Khan Bakai spoke thus,
He meant to lodge the guests overnight.
Your exhausted mother Chyiyrdy
Now prepared to begin her tale.
“My foal Bakai, hear my words!
Those great dogs attacked my caravan from Talas;
The boy upon my back is young—
I left without avenging myself upon the dogs.
The six villains openly plundered my property,
Digging pit after pit for me,
Blocking my road completely.
Once my own kin became enemies,
What sights those sons showed me!
I walked through pits and ravines;
My refuge was a cliff where no goat could graze.
My inheritance from my son Manas—
The forty companions—turned against me.
Calling them the sons Manas had left,
I tried to explain; they would not hear me.
The wretches shot their arrows down like rain,
Inflicting misery upon me.
Semetey, whose cradle is my leg,
Pokes my eyes like this.
Setting out toward Bukhara,
As I walked weeping in sorrow,
I found you in the wilderness.
Hear my words without growing weary.
I have many strange sights to tell of;
Open your eyes wide.
My great Bakai, my foal,
Hear my words without shame.
My gold became as coal.
The forty companions Magnanimous Manas left,
When the Magnanimous passed away,
Grown fat, laid waste my camp.
My silver was not worth coal.
When my beloved passed away,
Those great dogs, grown fat, blamed and attacked me.
My silk became as felt.
When my son passed away,
Those great dogs then destroyed my honor.
My kumys became sour water.
My Khizyr fled from over my head.
Your mother suffered persecution,
Becoming the talk of many peoples.
My foal Bakai, my leopard,
My spirits became bitter water.
After my six sons rose and plundered my camp,
I, once a gorge, became a road.
I, a khan's child, was abased.
I, who would not ride a trotting horse,
Was humbled to a sore-backed donkey.
I grew slow and weary.
Unable to ford the Syr Darya,
Unable to reach a known place,
My kin became my enemies.
My son Bakai, my anguish stayed within me.
Abyke and Kobosh, two villains—
From them I suffered humiliation.
Chyibyt and Kochkor, four villains—
From them I suffered humiliation.
Adybai and Kolbai, six villains—
From them I suffered violence.
Kyrgylchal at their head, and Tazbaimat—
From them I suffered tyranny.
My son Bakai, I have more to tell:
Abusing her with, ‘You refuse to marry!’
They brutalized dear Kanykei.
A drop flowing from Alai,
Cut across and across
By the whips the six villains dragged and struck.
My hero, Bakai my foal,
When bitter torment fell upon my head,
I had no strength to rely upon.
When the forty swine shouted and laid hands on us,
Watching from the ridge,
I had no renowned lion like you.
I had no cliff a goose could not circle,
No impregnable mountain like you.
This treacherous world, faithful as a hair is thin—
So this is what the shit-filled world is like!
Thinking, ‘Together they will find their chance;
Semetey, whose cradle is my leg,
Before he reaches his full strength,
Your dogs will hack apart.
They will camp along the little stream;
With this, my Manas
Will be like a fire put out.
The dogs will bring persecution’—
For this I came wandering away.
When they plundered my gold,
When the dogs inflicted torment,
When they raided my livestock,
When they joined to destroy me,
When they found their sure opportunity,
When they slashed the breast open,
I crept down Uch-Koshoi,
To Kaiypchy's Kara-Ungkur,
Carrying Semetey, my support,
And fled away to hide.
Unable to die, my eyes drooping,
My desolation showing,
My heart's very flesh in pain,
The soles of my feet rubbed raw,
Wearing a flapping felt cloak,
Stumbling across the wide steppe,
Suffering, my wretched eyes like embers,
My liver crushed and burning,
I had no mortal to help me.
Sobbing bitterly, travelling by night,
My son Bakai, I set out toward Bukhara,
Toward the ancient city of Bukhara.
My son Bakai, ruined, fleeing, wandering on foot,
Your friend's wife who has fled—
Kanykei bears no blame.
To soothe one's longing fully,
To fall into sound sleep,
There is no shelter where we can lie in peace,
No hollow in which to hide.
Your child left by your friend,
To give him even a little to eat,
There is no food or sustenance to keep us alive.
My days have shrivelled miserably.
Unable to reach a known place,
My back has grown bent,
My eyes have grown staring.
Only a spoonful of blood remains;
My flesh is utterly wasted.
Tears fill my eye sockets,
Pain fills my whole breast.
My joints have failed, my strength has gone;
My vigor ebbs, my senses swoon.
Black night has fallen over me.
I fear my orphan will die of hunger;
I fear his death will come today!
Leopard Bakai, my foal,
I have scattered—gather me up.
I have broken—join me together.
Kindle my extinguished fire;
Bring my dead soul back to life!
I am thirsty—quench my thirst.
I am weary—give my soul rest!
Do not press against my throat.
Khan Bakai, guard him as a father!
Nourish this wasted soul;
Fill this hungry belly.
Only son of the saintly old man,
I am thirsty—quench my thirst.
Give me six swift horses.
If you truly honor the departed spirit,
Khan Bakai, give me six skins of milk.
I have set out on a distant journey:
Give the only child a horse to ride away.
Khan Bakai, give a prayer against burning, give your aid.
Give a coat so we will not freeze to death.
So that our bellies will not hunger,
Give plenty of travel rations.
I have no strength to rely upon;
These words are addressed to you alone.
Give my soul a little rest.
“My renowned mother is fierce,” you say.
Fleeing Ken-Kol, running on foot,
I wept in grief and travelled by night.
Unable to reach a known place,
Khan Bakai, utterly helpless, I lay still.
The spring that flows from the hills—
May Allah Most High look kindly upon it.
Will he save this one,
The lamp the Magnanimous left behind!”
Draining Bakai's strength,
Your mother told him
Everything that had happened:
The humiliation Abyke inflicted,
The violence of Kobosh the slave,
The forty swine whom Manas left,
All forty, dog-swine from forty places,
How they plundered her possessions,
How thoroughly they wrought havoc.
When your mother had told him, sobbing,
When the tangled tale's knot
She had unravelled completely,
When the strife with which it began
She had recounted in full,
Your uncle Bakai, the precious khan—
Allah's sun clouded over in the sky;
Sixty cares came into his head.
His ribs seemed to part and split.
His precious eyes, like a saker falcon's,
Shed tears whenever he blinked.
Bakai dissolved in sobbing.
The bloody tears flowing from the noble hero's eyes
Poured down his beard.
His knees bent to the earth;
